chunks: "The usual choice is a half bridge with two N-channel MOSFETs and synchronous rectification.
The high-side NFET connects the switch node to V in , and the low-side NFET connects it to ground. They're driven complementary, with a little dead time between them.
There are two reasons. First, the low side is a FET instead of a diode because a diode drops a fixed 0. 3 to 0.
7 volts whenever the inductor current flows through it, while a FET drops I times R DS(on) , which can be tens of millivolts. On a 12 volts to 3.
3 volts converter at 2 amps, a Schottky wastes about 0. 65 watts out of 6. 6 watts, a 10 milliohm FET about 30 milliwatts.
And the lower the output voltage, the longer the low side conducts, so the win gets bigger.
Second, both are NFETs because for the same die area an NFET has about two to three times lower on-resistance than a PFET, since electrons are more mobile than holes.
Same resistance means a smaller, cheaper device with less gate charge and capacitance.
The price is that the high-side NFET needs a gate voltage above the input, so you need a bootstrap capacitor or charge pump, and you need dead-time control so the two FETs never conduct together."
